questions.question: Discuss the experimental evidence that led to the acceptance of the Chromosome Theory. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the experimental evidence that led to the acceptance of the
  • Chromosome Theory.
  • The Sutton and Boveri Theory, also known as the Chromosomal Theory
  • of Inheritance, was proposed by Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri in the
  • early 1900s. Genes are located on chromosomes, and these chromosomes
  • are responsible for passing traits from parents to offspring. Chromosomes
  • come in pairs – just like Mendel’s factors (genes). Chromosomes separate
  • during meiosis, like genes do in Mendel’s laws. Each parent gives one set
  • of chromosomes (and genes) to their child. (Liberal valuation)
  • [U] / [CO2]

questions.question: How can pedigree analysis be used to evaluate the ethical considerations of genetic counseling for a family with a history of haemophilia? / [CO4] [4x5 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• How can pedigree analysis be used to evaluate the ethical considerations ofgenetic counseling for a family with a history of haemophilia?
  • Haemophilia is a genetic bleeding disorder in which the blood does not
  • clot properly due to the absence or low levels of certain clotting factors. It
  • is usually inherited in anX-linkedrecessive pattern, meaning it primarily
  • affects males, while females are typically carriers. Pedigree analysis helps
  • trace how haemophilia is passed in a family. Pedigree analysis helps
  • identify carriers and affected individuals, enabling family members to
  • make informed choices about reproduction, prenatal testing, or early
  • treatment options. It is useful in genetic counselling to: Find out who may
  • carry or get the disease, help families make informed choices about
  • having children, keep family information private, avoid pressure—
  • counselors only guide, not force decisions, Prevent harm by planning
  • ahead for care or treatment. By clarifying genetic risks through analysis,
  • counselors can help prevent misconceptions and reduce the risk of social
  • stigma or genetic discrimination within families or communities. (Brief
  • Description - Any four relevant points- 4 marks)
  • [An] / [CO4]
  • [4x5=20Marks]
